subject: Mapping hybrid traffic profiles to queueing headroom for private GPU pools
messages:
From: Alex Chen <eng@acme.ai>
To: rafael_mendes <rafael@redwood.com>
Cc: platform@edgecloud.com
Date: Mon, 22 Jul 2029 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: [Request] Hybrid traffic mix and headroom guidance for our private pool

Hi Rafael,

Thanks for taking time to review our private deployment requirements. Were planning a VPC deployment that will ingest traffic both from our mobile edge (via EdgeCloud peering) and from internal web clients in us-east. We expect a steady daytime baseline of ~700 qps for text-generation (average prompt length ~120 tokens) with frequent user-driven bursts to ~3.5k qps during marketing peaks. Additionally, the edge path will have short high-frequency spikes (100-200 qps) that are latency-sensitive (95p target < 120ms).

Key asks:
- Can Redwood recommend queue depth and admission-control thresholds for a private GPU pool sized for this hybrid mix?
- What warm-pool sizing and cache prefill strategy do you recommend so that edge spikes remain low-latency?
- Network egress limits: were targeting a 40 Gbps interconnect between our VPC and EdgeCloud. Will that be a bottleneck for the requested bursts?

I attached our coarse traffic_profile and a brief network map. Happy to jump on a call later this week.

Thanks,
Alex Chen
Senior Platform Engineer, Acme AI
Attachment: acme_traffic_profile_v1.csv (CSV)
Attachment: vpc_network_map_v2.png (PNG)
From: rafael_mendes <rafael@redwood.com>

Cc: jonas_weber <jonas@redwood.com>, laura_bennett <laura@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: [Request] Hybrid traffic mix and headroom guidance for our private pool

Alex,

Thanks for the details and the attachments — helpful. High level thoughts below; Ive copied Jonas and Laura to align on operational constraints and provisioning cadence. I also attached a short calc workbook with an initial headroom recommendation.

Short answers up front:
- Admission control + small warm pool is the right tradeoff for your mix. Plan for ~40% headroom above sustained baseline and autoscale to absorb most marketing peaks, with a hard admission cap for extreme tails.
- Warm-pool sizing: keep roughly 8-12% of total GPUs in a warm state for low-latency edge spikes (fast-path instances pinned with warmed KV).
- Network: a single 40 Gbps egress can be hit during simultaneous maximum bursts; youll want multi-link or burst shaper rules to avoid head-of-line blocking for latency-sensitive flows.

I outlined a first-pass model in the attached spreadsheet (queueing_headroom_calc.xlsx) — it converts your qps and token distributions into expected GPU token/sec, allocates batch sizes by latency SLO, and yields a recommended GPU count and admission thresholds.

Next steps:
1) Jonas to propose autoscale policy windows (warmup, cooldown) and burst admission curve.
2) Laura to confirm networking topology constraints and whether multi-link is available.
3) Schedule a 30-min technical sync with EdgeCloud to validate peering QoS.

Cheers,
Rafael Mendes
Head of Solutions Engineering, Redwood Inference

From: jonas_weber <jonas@redwood.com>

Cc: laura_bennett <laura@redwood.com>, mina_haddad <mina@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 23 Jul 2029 08:30:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: [Request] Hybrid traffic mix and headroom guidance for our private pool

Alex / team,

I pulled the numbers and sketched an operational model. Key assumptions: 1 GPU (A100-class) can sustain ~1200 short-context tokens/sec with 8-16 token average generation latency at small batch sizes; effective throughput varies with quantization and batching. Using your average prompt length (120 tokens) and target latency (95p < 120ms), I propose the following conservative sizing:

- Sustained baseline: 700 qps * 120 tokens = 84k tokens/sec -> ~70 GPU-equivalent sustained tokens/sec required (84k / 1200 ~= 70).
- Peak marketing bursts: 3.5k qps -> 420k tokens/sec -> ~350 GPUs to fully absorb at baseline kernel efficiency.
- Desired headroom: plan for 40% operational headroom above baseline (sustained) so baseline should provision ~98 GPU equivalents.
- Warm pool: 10% of provisioned GPUs (round up) pinned in warmed process state for fast KV access and minimal cold-start penalty -> ~10 GPUs warmed when at baseline.

Autoscale policy (proposal):
- Scale up when 1-min moving average of queue depth > 25% of buffer for 60s.
- Scale down after 10-minute cooldown and when 5-min moving average falls < 15% buffer.
- Burst admission curve: allow spikes up to 120% of provisioned capacity for 30s (best effort), then start shedding low-priority/async requests. Latency-sensitive edge traffic should be tagged and prioritized.

Network note: 40 Gbps equals ~5GB/s. During the 3.5k qps burst with average response payload of 2.5kB, bandwidth can approach ~8.7MB/s per 1k qps — multiplied out, worst-case egress can exceed 40Gbps if many responses are large. Recommend per-flow shapers and an optional second 40Gbps link for burst absorption.

Ill add these numbers to the workbook and label the scenarios. Mina, can you validate whether a 1200 tokens/sec GPU is realistic for Acmes model family (7B quantized)? If not, well revise.

- Jonas

From: Mina Haddad <mina@redwood.com>
To: jonas_weber <jonas@redwood.com>, rafael_mendes <rafael@redwood.com>, Alex Chen <eng@acme.ai>
Cc: laura_bennett <laura@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 23 Jul 2029 11:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: [Request] Hybrid traffic mix and headroom guidance for our private pool

Quick validation from ML infra: 1200 tokens/sec per GPU is achievable for a quantized 7B family with batch sizes <= 8 and short context optimization, but only if:
- KV cache warm state is maintained between related requests,
- Batching windows are tuned to 10-20ms for edge flows,
- Mixed-precision kernels are enabled and memory pinning is used.

If Acmes model uses longer context (e.g., 1k+), throughput drops significantly; please confirm typical sequence lengths for the generative tail. Also, cold-start penalty for a cold process can be ~200-400ms depending on model warmup; that motivates the warm pool strategy.

Action items:
- Alex: confirm max response size (bytes) and tail-context frequency.
- Laura: confirm whether Acme can provision a second cross-connect or implement per-flow policing on the existing 40Gbps link.
- Rafael/Jonas: we should produce a short runbook describing admission-control signals and how to tag latency-sensitive requests for priority scheduling.

Mina Haddad
Principal Applied ML Infra, Redwood Inference

Team,

Thanks — that level of detail is exactly what we needed. Quick answers:
- Typical response payload is ~2.2kB; long-context (1k+ tokens) is rare (~2% of requests) but can happen in analytic flows.
- We can open a second 40Gbps cross-connect but need to validate procurement timelines; will aim to have it within the quarter.

Next steps for us: schedule the 30-min sync with EdgeCloud (were available Thu/Fri), finalize the workbook, and get the runbook for admission-control so our SREs can simulate the admission curve.

I attached an updated traffic profile with percentiles for response size.

Appreciate the quick turnaround.

—Alex
